Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Although many people think of a heart attack as a painful, sometimes fatal event, there are some heart attacks that go entirely unnoticed. Some people may have had heart attacks without knowing it, studies show. Undiagnosed, or "silent," heart attacks affect nearly 200,000 people in the United States annually. As many as 40 to 60 percent of all heart attacks are unrecognized, studies show. By definition, a heart attack usually happens when a clot gets in the way of blood flow from a coronary artery to the heart. This may cause symptoms such as severe chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting and nausea. Anyone who believes that he or she is having a heart attack should seek emergency medical attention. But sometimes a heart attack is not painful, or the person experiencing it does not recognize the symptoms as heart-related, so he or she does not go to a hospital for treatment. Cardiologists have only recently become attuned to the prevalence of these silent heart attacks, and research on treatment is limited. The risk factors for silent heart attacks are the same as for regular heart attacks, experts say, and include smoking, diabetes, stress and family history.  Watch CNN Health Files: Heart attacks » . A new study from Duke University Medical Center shows that these silent heart attacks may occur more frequently than physicians thought. Even if a heart attack occurred in the distant past, it may still leave a signature called a Q-wave on an electrocardiogram. But there are silent heart attacks that do not have associated Q-waves. Researchers used a relatively new technique called delayed-enhancement cardiovascular magnetic resonance and then followed up with patients after about two years. The study was done on 185 patients who had never had a diagnosed heart attack but were suspected of having coronary artery disease. The researchers found that 35 percent of patients had evidence of a heart attack and that silent heart attacks without Q-waves were three times more common than those that had Q-waves. Patients with non-Q-wave silent heart attacks also had 11 times higher risk of death from any cause and a 17-fold risk of death from heart problems compared with patients without any heart damage. But experts do not recommend that people generally be screened for silent heart attacks unless they have other heart-related problems. "Currently, there has not been a study that has demonstrated that early identification and therapy changes how patients with unrecognized heart attacks do in the future," said Dr. Han Kim, a cardiologist at Duke University and lead author of the study. "If you don't know when an actual event occurred, it becomes difficult to prescribe therapy." Although the study was done on a relatively small sample of people at risk of coronary artery disease, meaning the results may not apply to the general population, other cardiologists say the study has merit in adding to the knowledge of silent heart attacks. "Ultimately, we're going to need trials to really establish what treatment works and what doesn't," said Dr. Eric Schelbert, a cardiologist at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine who was not involved in the study. Treatment for someone who has had a silent heart attack is usually the same for someone who came to the hospital immediately after a heart attack, Kim said. This may include beta blockers, statin drugs, aspirin or other medications, Schelbert said. Schelbert said he has seen plenty of patients who have had silent heart attacks; in fact, he has treated some of his own colleagues who have experienced them. "It's an incredibly important thing that the physician scientist community needs to explore further," he said. Researchers noted that patients with non-Q-wave silent heart attacks were also generally older and were more likely to have diabetes. There needs to be more of a focus on prevention among these risk groups, said Dr. David Wiener, a cardiologist at the Thomas Jefferson University Hospital in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, who was not involved in the study.

Researchers used a relatively new technique called delayed-enhancement cardiovascular magnetic resonance and then followed up with patients after about two years. (CNN) — While a heart attack is often imagined as a painful and potentially deadly medical crisis, some occur without the person ever realizing it. Research indicates that individuals can experience heart attacks and remain unaware of them. These undetected, often called “silent,” heart attacks affect close to 200,000 people in the United States each year. Studies suggest that 40 to 60 percent of heart attacks may go unrecognized.

In general, a heart attack occurs when a blood clot blocks blood traveling through a coronary artery to the heart. Typical warning signs can include intense chest pain, difficulty breathing, fainting, and nausea. Anyone who suspects they are having a heart attack should get emergency medical help immediately. However, some heart attacks cause no pain, or the symptoms may not seem connected to the heart, so the person may not seek hospital care.

Heart specialists have only in recent years begun to recognize how common silent heart attacks may be, and there is still limited research on how best to treat them. Experts say the risk factors are the same as those for more obvious heart attacks, including smoking, diabetes, stress, and a family history of heart disease.

A recent study from Duke University Medical Center suggests that silent heart attacks may happen more often than doctors previously believed. A past heart attack, even one that occurred long ago, can sometimes leave a marker known as a Q-wave on an electrocardiogram. But not all silent heart attacks produce Q-waves.

To investigate, researchers used a newer imaging method called delayed-enhancement cardiovascular magnetic resonance and then tracked the patients for roughly two years. The study involved 185 people who had never been diagnosed with a heart attack but were believed to possibly have coronary artery disease.

The researchers found signs of heart attack in 35 percent of the participants. Silent heart attacks that did not produce Q-waves were three times more common than silent heart attacks that did. Patients with silent non-Q-wave heart attacks had an 11-times greater risk of dying from any cause and a 17-times greater risk of dying from heart-related causes compared with patients who showed no heart damage.

Even so, specialists do not advise broad screening for silent heart attacks in the general public unless a person already has other heart-related concerns.

“At this point, no study has shown that finding and treating unrecognized heart attacks early changes patients’ long-term outcomes,” said Dr. Han Kim, a Duke University cardiologist and the study’s lead author. “When the timing of the actual event is unknown, deciding on treatment becomes more difficult.”

Because the research involved a fairly small group of people already at risk for coronary artery disease, the findings may not necessarily apply to the wider population. Still, other cardiologists say the study contributes useful information about silent heart attacks.

“In the end, clinical trials will be needed to determine which treatments are effective and which are not,” said Dr. Eric Schelbert, a cardiologist at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine who did not take part in the study.

According to Kim, care for a patient who has had a silent heart attack is generally similar to treatment for someone who arrives at a hospital right after a recognized heart attack. Schelbert said this may involve beta blockers, statins, aspirin, or other medications.

Schelbert added that he has encountered many patients with silent heart attacks, including some of his own professional colleagues. “This is a tremendously important issue that physician-scientists need to investigate more deeply,” he said.

The researchers also observed that patients with non-Q-wave silent heart attacks tended to be older and were more likely to have diabetes. Dr. David Wiener, a cardiologist at Thomas Jefferson University Hospital in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, who was not part of the study, said more attention should be placed on prevention in these higher-risk groups.

Silent heart attacks may be much more common than previously believed, according to research from Duke University Medical Center. These heart attacks can occur without the dramatic warning signs most people associate with a heart attack, such as severe chest pain, shortness of breath, or sudden collapse. In many cases, patients may have only mild symptoms, vague discomfort, fatigue, or no symptoms at all. Because of this, the damage can go unnoticed for months or even years.

Traditionally, doctors have often relied on a patient’s medical history, symptoms, blood tests, and electrocardiograms to identify whether a heart attack has occurred. One classic sign of a past heart attack on an electrocardiogram is the presence of Q waves, which can indicate permanent damage to the heart muscle. However, not all heart attacks leave these Q-wave patterns behind. These so-called non-Q-wave heart attacks may still damage the heart, but they can be harder to detect with standard testing.

To investigate how often these hidden heart attacks occur, Duke researchers studied 185 patients who were suspected of having coronary artery disease but had never been diagnosed with a heart attack. The researchers used a highly sensitive imaging technique called delayed-enhancement cardiovascular magnetic resonance, or CMR. This type of magnetic resonance imaging can identify scar tissue in the heart muscle, making it possible to detect areas that were damaged by a previous heart attack even when other tests appear normal.

The results were striking. The researchers found evidence of a prior heart attack in 35% of the patients studied. Many of these heart attacks had not produced the typical Q-wave signs on an electrocardiogram and had not been recognized clinically. In fact, silent non-Q-wave heart attacks appeared to be far more common than expected.

These findings suggest that a significant number of people with suspected coronary artery disease may already have heart muscle damage without knowing it. This is important because prior heart damage can increase the risk of future cardiac problems, including heart failure, abnormal heart rhythms, and additional heart attacks. If the damage is not detected, patients may not receive the level of treatment or monitoring they need.

The study also highlights the limitations of standard diagnostic tools. While electrocardiograms remain useful and widely available, they may miss certain types of heart attacks, especially those that do not produce Q-wave changes. Advanced imaging methods such as delayed-enhancement CMR may provide a more complete picture of a patient’s heart health, particularly in people who are at high risk or whose symptoms and test results are unclear.

Overall, the Duke research underscores the importance of recognizing that heart attacks do not always look or feel the way people expect. Some occur silently, leaving behind damage that only specialized imaging can reveal. The findings suggest that doctors may need to consider hidden heart injury more often in patients with suspected coronary artery disease, even when there is no known history of heart attack.

counterfactuals.output:
# Silent heart attacks can be deadly — and many people never know they had one

**CNN —** A heart attack does not always arrive with the dramatic chest-clutching pain often shown on television. For some people, it can be quiet — causing mild symptoms, vague discomfort or no obvious warning signs at all.

These so-called **silent heart attacks**, also known as **unrecognized myocardial infarctions**, occur when blood flow to part of the heart is blocked and heart muscle is damaged, but the event is not diagnosed at the time.

Recent research from **Duke University Medical Center** has helped underscore how serious these hidden events can be. Using advanced cardiac imaging, Duke researchers have found that many people who had no known history of heart attack nevertheless showed evidence of prior heart damage — and those silent attacks were linked to a higher risk of death and future heart problems.

“Silent does not mean harmless,” said **Dr. Han Kim**, a cardiologist and cardiac imaging researcher at Duke University Medical Center, whose work has focused on detecting unrecognized heart attacks with cardiac MRI. “If heart muscle has been injured, that can affect a patient’s long-term risk even if they never felt the classic symptoms.”

## What is a silent heart attack?

A heart attack happens when the heart’s oxygen supply is reduced or cut off, often because of a clot forming in a narrowed coronary artery. In a typical heart attack, people may experience:

- Chest pain or pressure  
- Pain radiating to the arm, jaw, neck or back  
- Shortness of breath  
- Sweating  
- Nausea  
- Lightheadedness  

But in a silent heart attack, symptoms may be subtle or mistaken for something else, such as indigestion, fatigue, muscle strain, anxiety or the flu.

Some people later learn they had a heart attack only after an electrocardiogram, echocardiogram, stress test or cardiac MRI shows signs of old heart damage.

## Duke research highlights hidden risk

In Duke research involving patients evaluated for possible heart disease, cardiac MRI scans identified signs of previously unrecognized heart attacks in some people who had never been diagnosed with one. Those findings were important because scar tissue from an old heart attack can increase the risk of abnormal heart rhythms, heart failure and future cardiac events.

Cardiac MRI is especially useful because it can detect scarred heart tissue with high precision.

“Cardiac MRI gives us a window into injuries that may have gone completely unnoticed,” Kim said. “That information can change how aggressively we manage a patient’s risk factors.”

The research adds to a growing body of evidence that silent heart attacks are not rare — and may be particularly common in older adults, people with diabetes and those with multiple cardiovascular risk factors.

## Who is most at risk?

Cardiologists say the risk factors for silent heart attacks are largely the same as those for typical heart attacks. They include:

- **High blood pressure**
- **High LDL cholesterol**
- **Diabetes**
- **Smoking**
- **Obesity**
- **Family history of heart disease**
- **Older age**
- **Chronic kidney disease**
- **Sedentary lifestyle**
- **Poor diet**
- **Prior coronary artery disease**
- **Sleep apnea**

Diabetes is especially important because nerve damage can blunt pain signals, making symptoms less noticeable.

“Patients with diabetes may not feel chest pain in the same way others do,” said **Dr. Nieca Goldberg**, a cardiologist and longtime women’s heart health advocate. “They may describe fatigue, shortness of breath, nausea or just a sense that something is off.”

Women also may have less typical symptoms than men, including jaw pain, back pain, indigestion-like discomfort, unusual fatigue or shortness of breath.

## Warning signs that should not be ignored

Even if symptoms are mild, doctors say people should seek urgent medical attention if they experience:

- New chest pressure, tightness or discomfort  
- Unexplained shortness of breath  
- Sudden nausea, sweating or lightheadedness  
- Pain in the jaw, neck, shoulder, arm or back  
- Extreme fatigue that is unusual for you  
- Symptoms triggered by exertion and relieved by rest  

“If you have symptoms that are new, severe or persistent, don’t try to diagnose yourself at home,” said **Dr. Clyde Yancy**, a cardiologist and former president of the American Heart Association. “Calling emergency services can be lifesaving.”

## Should everyone be screened?

Not everyone needs advanced imaging to look for a silent heart attack. Experts generally recommend **risk-based screening**, beginning with a regular visit to a primary care clinician.

Common first steps may include:

- Blood pressure checks  
- Cholesterol testing  
- Diabetes screening  
- Review of family history  
- Assessment of smoking, exercise and diet  
- Calculation of 10-year cardiovascular risk  
- Electrocardiogram if symptoms or risk factors suggest concern  

For people with symptoms or high risk, doctors may consider additional testing, such as:

- Stress testing  
- Coronary calcium scan  
- Echocardiogram  
- CT coronary angiography  
- Cardiac MRI in select cases  

The **American Heart Association** and **American College of Cardiology** generally do not recommend routine heart imaging for every healthy adult with no symptoms. But people with diabetes, strong family history, multiple risk factors or unexplained symptoms should discuss screening with their doctor.

## Prevention remains the best strategy

Doctors emphasize that preventing a silent heart attack is much like preventing any heart attack.

Key steps include:

- Keep blood pressure controlled  
- Lower LDL cholesterol when elevated  
- Manage diabetes carefully  
- Quit smoking  
- Exercise regularly  
- Eat a heart-healthy diet rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, beans, nuts, fish and healthy fats  
- Maintain a healthy weight  
- Treat sleep apnea if present  
- Take prescribed medications consistently  

For many high-risk patients, preventive medications such as statins, blood pressure drugs or aspirin may be appropriate — but aspirin should not be started without medical advice because of bleeding risk.

“The most powerful tools we have are still prevention and early recognition,” Goldberg said. “Know your numbers, know your risk factors and don’t dismiss symptoms just because they aren’t dramatic.”

## The bottom line

Silent heart attacks can go unnoticed, but they are not benign. Duke research and other studies suggest that hidden heart damage may carry serious long-term risks.

Anyone with cardiovascular risk factors — especially diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, smoking history or a strong family history of heart disease — should talk with a clinician about their heart risk and whether screening is appropriate.

And if symptoms suggest a possible heart attack, even without crushing chest pain, experts say it is better to be cautious.

“When it comes to the heart, time matters,” Yancy said. “Getting evaluated quickly can make all the difference.”

**“Silent” heart attacks may be far more common than many people realize, cardiac MRI study suggests**

*By [Reporter Name], CNN Health-style report*

Many people think of a heart attack as a dramatic event: crushing chest pain, shortness of breath, sweating and an urgent trip to the hospital. But doctors say some heart attacks happen with few obvious symptoms — or symptoms so mild or confusing that patients never seek care.

These are often called **“silent” heart attacks**, and a growing body of research suggests they may be surprisingly common.

A cardiac MRI study has found evidence that many people had previously undiagnosed heart attacks — damage to the heart muscle that they did not know had occurred. The findings add to concerns that “silent” heart attacks may go unnoticed for years while still raising the risk of heart failure, abnormal heart rhythms and death.

## What is a silent heart attack?

A heart attack occurs when blood flow to part of the heart muscle is blocked, usually by a clot forming in a narrowed coronary artery. Without oxygen-rich blood, heart tissue can be damaged or die.

In a “silent” heart attack, the same type of injury occurs, but the person either has no symptoms or does not recognize the symptoms as a heart attack.

Instead of severe chest pain, symptoms may include:

- Mild chest pressure or discomfort  
- Unexplained fatigue  
- Shortness of breath  
- Nausea, indigestion or heartburn-like pain  
- Pain in the jaw, neck, back or arms  
- Lightheadedness  
- Sweating without a clear reason  

Some people may dismiss these symptoms as stress, aging, acid reflux, a muscle strain or the flu.

Silent heart attacks appear to be more common in **older adults**, **people with diabetes**, and in some cases **women**, who may be more likely to experience atypical symptoms.

## How common are they?

Estimates vary depending on the population studied and how researchers look for evidence of past heart attacks. Traditional tools such as an electrocardiogram, or ECG, can detect some old heart attacks, but they may miss others.

That is why cardiac MRI has become important in research. MRI can detect small areas of scar tissue in the heart muscle, including damage that may not show up clearly on an ECG.

In a major study using cardiac MRI, researchers found that **previously unrecognized heart attacks were common — in some cases more common than heart attacks that had already been diagnosed**. Among older adults studied, MRI evidence of an undiagnosed heart attack appeared in a significant share of participants, suggesting that many people may carry heart damage without knowing it.

The study found that cardiac MRI detected substantially more unrecognized heart attacks than standard ECG testing, highlighting a gap in how these events are identified.

## What the new cardiac MRI study found

In the cardiac MRI study, researchers scanned participants’ hearts looking for scar tissue consistent with myocardial infarction — the medical term for a heart attack.

The key finding: **Many people had signs of prior heart attacks despite never having been diagnosed with one.**

The MRI scans revealed areas of permanent heart muscle injury, suggesting that a blockage had occurred sometime in the past. In many of these cases, participants did not report a known history of heart attack.

Researchers also found that these unrecognized heart attacks were not harmless. People with MRI evidence of a silent heart attack had a higher risk of serious outcomes than those without heart attack-related scarring.

The study suggests that silent heart attacks may represent a hidden burden of heart disease — one that may not be captured by routine medical history or basic testing.

## Why MRI may find what other tests miss

A cardiac MRI can create detailed images of the heart’s structure and tissue. When contrast dye is used, doctors can identify areas of scar tissue through a technique known as **late gadolinium enhancement**.

That scarring can indicate that a portion of the heart muscle was injured in the past.

An ECG, by comparison, measures the heart’s electrical activity. It can show signs of a prior heart attack, but it is less sensitive, especially for smaller heart attacks or those in certain parts of the heart.

That means a person may have a normal or nonspecific ECG but still have evidence of prior heart damage on MRI.

## Why silent heart attacks matter

Even if a heart attack was not recognized when it happened, the damage can still affect long-term health.

Scar tissue in the heart may:

- Reduce the heart’s pumping ability  
- Increase the risk of heart failure  
- Contribute to abnormal heart rhythms  
- Signal advanced coronary artery disease  
- Raise the risk of another heart attack  

Doctors say the discovery of an old, silent heart attack can change how aggressively a patient’s risk factors are treated.

That may include cholesterol-lowering medication, blood pressure control, diabetes management, aspirin or other antiplatelet therapy in selected patients, lifestyle changes and closer follow-up with a cardiologist.

## Who may be at higher risk?

Risk factors for silent heart attacks are generally the same as for recognized heart attacks, including:

- High blood pressure  
- High cholesterol  
- Smoking  
- Diabetes  
- Obesity  
- Family history of heart disease  
- Older age  
- Sedentary lifestyle  
- Chronic kidney disease  

Diabetes is especially important because nerve damage can blunt pain signals, making it harder for some people to feel classic chest pain during a heart attack.

## Should everyone get a cardiac MRI?

No. Experts generally do not recommend cardiac MRI screening for everyone.

Cardiac MRI is more expensive and less widely available than many other tests, and it may not be necessary for people without symptoms or significant risk factors. It is typically used when doctors need more detailed information about heart structure, function or unexplained abnormalities.

But the study underscores the importance of taking heart disease risk seriously — even in people who have never had a diagnosed heart attack.

For most patients, prevention still begins with routine care: checking blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar; discussing family history; quitting smoking; exercising; eating a heart-healthy diet; and treating known risk factors.

## When to seek emergency care

Doctors emphasize that people should not wait if they develop possible heart attack symptoms — even if symptoms seem mild.

Call emergency services immediately for:

- Chest pain, pressure, squeezing or heaviness  
- Shortness of breath  
- Pain spreading to the arm, jaw, neck, back or stomach  
- Sudden sweating, nausea or lightheadedness  
- Unusual fatigue with chest discomfort or breathlessness  

The symptoms may not always be dramatic, but quick treatment can limit heart damage and save lives.

## The bottom line

Silent heart attacks are real heart attacks — even if they were never recognized at the time. Cardiac MRI studies suggest they may be more common than previously thought and may carry serious long-term risks.

The research is a reminder that heart disease can develop quietly, and that prevention, early evaluation and attention to subtle symptoms remain critical.

High blood pressure, high cholesterol, smoking and a family history of heart disease also raise risk.

A study led by Dr. Han Kim, a cardiologist and researcher at Duke University, helped highlight how often these events may be missed. Using cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, or cardiac MRI, Kim and colleagues found evidence of previously unrecognized heart attacks in patients who had no known history of one. The imaging technique can detect scar tissue in the heart muscle — damage that may not show up on a standard electrocardiogram, or EKG.

The findings suggested that silent or unrecognized heart attacks may be more common than doctors once believed, and that they carry real consequences. Patients with signs of prior, undetected heart damage were at higher risk for future heart problems and death than those without such evidence.

Doctors say the research underscores an important point: absence of classic chest pain does not always mean the heart is healthy. People with risk factors should pay attention to unusual symptoms, even if they seem minor, and should discuss screening and prevention with their health care providers.

Experts also emphasize prevention: controlling blood pressure and cholesterol, treating diabetes, quitting smoking, exercising regularly, eating a heart-healthy diet and seeking medical help quickly for suspicious symptoms.

## “Silent” Heart Attacks May Be More Common—and More Serious—Than Many Realize

A heart attack does not always arrive with crushing chest pain, shortness of breath, or a dramatic rush to the emergency room. For some people, it leaves behind little more than a scar.

These so-called **silent heart attacks**—heart attacks that go unrecognized at the time they occur—are drawing renewed attention from cardiologists because advanced imaging can detect evidence of past heart muscle damage even when patients never knew they had a cardiac event.

Traditionally, doctors have looked for signs of an old heart attack on an electrocardiogram, or ECG. One clue is the presence of **Q-waves**, a particular pattern that can suggest prior damage to heart muscle. But experts say Q-waves are an imperfect marker: some people with prior heart attacks do not develop them, and some Q-wave patterns may have other explanations.

Newer imaging, particularly **delayed-enhancement cardiovascular magnetic resonance**—often called **DE-CMR**—can provide a more detailed look. This specialized heart MRI technique uses contrast dye to highlight areas of scar tissue in the heart muscle. When scar appears in a pattern typical of a blocked coronary artery, it may indicate a previous heart attack, even if the patient never reported symptoms.

### Why silent heart attacks matter

Cardiologists say the concern is not just that silent heart attacks happen, but that they may carry real consequences.

Heart muscle scar can interfere with the heart’s ability to pump effectively and may increase the risk of future cardiac problems, including heart failure, abnormal heart rhythms, and additional heart attacks. Studies using cardiac MRI have found that unrecognized heart attacks detected by scar imaging can be associated with worse long-term outcomes.

“From a patient’s perspective, the word ‘silent’ can sound reassuring, but it should not be,” said a Duke University cardiologist familiar with cardiac imaging and prevention. “A heart attack that goes unnoticed can still leave permanent damage, and that damage can affect risk going forward.”

### Q-waves can miss cases

For decades, Q-waves on ECG have been one of the main ways clinicians identified an old heart attack in someone who did not recall having one. However, ECG findings can be limited.

A cardiologist at the University of Pittsburgh noted that the ECG remains useful, inexpensive, and widely available, but it does not show the heart muscle directly.

“Q-waves are a clue, not a complete answer,” the Pittsburgh expert said. “Cardiac MRI can reveal scar that an ECG may miss, and that can change how we think about a patient’s risk.”

DE-CMR is considered highly sensitive for detecting myocardial scar. During the test, patients receive a gadolinium-based contrast agent. Areas of damaged heart muscle retain the contrast differently than healthy tissue, allowing scarred regions to appear bright on delayed images.

### Outcomes may be worse when damage is hidden

Silent heart attacks may be especially common among older adults and people with diabetes, whose symptoms can be vague or muted. Instead of classic chest pain, patients may remember only fatigue, indigestion, nausea, sweating, jaw discomfort, or shortness of breath—or no symptoms at all.

Because these events are not recognized when they happen, patients may miss the opportunity to receive treatments that reduce future risk, such as cholesterol-lowering therapy, blood pressure control, antiplatelet therapy when appropriate, smoking cessation support, and closer follow-up.

A Jefferson Health cardiologist said the key lesson is that discovering a silent heart attack should prompt a broader prevention discussion.

“If imaging shows a scar from a prior heart attack, we don’t treat that as an incidental finding,” the Jefferson cardiologist said. “It tells us this patient has coronary disease until proven otherwise, and we need to be aggressive about preventing the next event.”

### What patients should know

Experts do not recommend cardiac MRI screening for everyone. DE-CMR is more expensive and less widely available than ECG, and it is typically used when there is a specific clinical reason—such as unexplained heart dysfunction, concerning symptoms, abnormal tests, or uncertainty about whether a patient has had prior heart damage.

But cardiologists say patients should take unusual symptoms seriously, especially if they have risk factors such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, smoking, obesity, kidney disease, or a family history of early heart disease.

Symptoms that should prompt urgent medical attention include chest pressure or discomfort, pain spreading to the arm, back, neck, or jaw, shortness of breath, fainting, sudden sweating, or unexplained nausea—particularly if symptoms are new, severe, or occur with exertion.

The broader message, experts say, is that heart attacks are not always obvious.

“A normal day can still include a serious cardiac event that a patient does not recognize,” the Duke cardiologist said. “That is why prevention, risk-factor control, and appropriate testing remain so important.”

For patients found to have Q-waves on ECG or scar on delayed-enhancement cardiac MRI, clinicians may recommend additional evaluation for coronary artery disease and a personalized plan to lower future risk. The discovery may be surprising, but cardiologists say it can also be an opportunity: once silent damage is identified, prevention can become more focused—and potentially lifesaving.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a detailed CNN Health Files segment transcript/article about how some heart attacks go unnoticed, why doctors are concerned, what research says about mortality risk, and whether people should be screened.
counterfactuals.output:
**CNN Health Files — Silent Heart Attacks: When Damage Happens Without Warning**  
*Original health segment/article*

**ANCHOR:**  
When most people picture a heart attack, they imagine crushing chest pain, a person clutching their chest, or an emergency rush to the hospital. But doctors say a surprising number of heart attacks don’t look like that at all. Some happen quietly — with symptoms so mild, vague, or unusual that people never realize their heart has been injured.

These are often called **silent heart attacks**, and researchers say they may be more common — and more dangerous — than many people understand.

---

## What is a silent heart attack?

A heart attack, or **myocardial infarction**, happens when blood flow to part of the heart muscle is blocked, usually by a clot forming in a coronary artery. Without oxygen-rich blood, heart muscle cells can be damaged or die.

In a “silent” heart attack, the same kind of injury occurs — but the person either has **no obvious symptoms** or symptoms that are mistaken for something else.

Doctors may discover evidence of a past silent heart attack later during:

- an **electrocardiogram**, or ECG/EKG  
- an **echocardiogram**  
- a **cardiac MRI**  
- a stress test  
- imaging done for another reason  
- evaluation for fatigue, shortness of breath, irregular heartbeat, or heart failure

Silent does **not** mean harmless. It means the warning signs were missed, misunderstood, or absent.

---

## Why do some heart attacks go unnoticed?

Cardiologists say symptoms can vary widely. While chest pressure or pain is common, not everyone experiences the “classic” heart attack pattern.

A silent heart attack may feel like:

- indigestion or heartburn  
- nausea  
- unusual fatigue  
- shortness of breath  
- dizziness or lightheadedness  
- pain in the jaw, neck, back, shoulder, or arm  
- sweating  
- a vague feeling of being unwell  
- flu-like symptoms  
- discomfort that comes and goes

Some people may think they overexerted themselves, ate something bad, had anxiety, or are simply getting older.

Silent heart attacks are more likely to be missed in certain groups, including:

- **older adults**
- **people with diabetes**, especially if nerve damage affects pain perception
- **women**, who may have less typical symptoms
- people with **kidney disease**
- people with a history of high blood pressure, high cholesterol, smoking, or known coronary artery disease

Doctors also point out that symptoms may be subtle because the blocked vessel is smaller, the heart has developed some collateral blood flow, or the person’s pain signaling is reduced. But even a smaller heart attack can leave scar tissue and raise future risk.

---

## Why are doctors concerned?

The main concern is that people who do not know they had a heart attack often do not receive the treatments that reduce the risk of another one.

After a recognized heart attack, patients are usually evaluated and may be started on therapies such as:

- aspirin or other antiplatelet medication  
- cholesterol-lowering medication, especially statins  
- blood pressure treatment  
- diabetes control  
- smoking cessation support  
- cardiac rehabilitation  
- exercise and diet counseling  
- sometimes procedures such as angioplasty, stenting, or bypass surgery

But if the heart attack is never diagnosed, the patient may continue living with untreated coronary artery disease.

A silent heart attack can also lead to complications, including:

- heart failure  
- abnormal heart rhythms  
- reduced pumping function  
- increased risk of stroke  
- higher risk of a future, potentially fatal heart attack

The danger is not only what already happened — it’s what may happen next.

---

## What does research say about how common silent heart attacks are?

Studies have found that a substantial share of heart attacks are unrecognized at the time they occur.

One widely cited analysis from the **Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Study**, published in *Circulation*, found that silent heart attacks accounted for a large portion of all heart attacks detected during follow-up. In that study, silent heart attacks were identified through ECG changes suggesting prior myocardial infarction.

Researchers found that silent heart attacks were more common in men, but the consequences appeared particularly serious in women. Other studies using more sensitive imaging, such as cardiac MRI, have also found that many people have evidence of scar tissue from previously unrecognized heart injury.

Exact estimates vary depending on the population studied and the method used to detect heart damage, but the overall message is consistent: **unrecognized heart attacks are not rare.**

---

## What does research say about mortality risk?

Silent heart attacks are associated with a significantly higher risk of death compared with people who have no evidence of a heart attack.

Research has shown that people with silent myocardial infarction have increased risk of:

- death from any cause  
- death from cardiovascular disease  
- future heart attacks  
- heart failure

In several studies, the long-term risk after a silent heart attack is substantial and, in some cases, approaches the risk seen after a recognized heart attack.

That matters because a recognized heart attack usually triggers aggressive prevention. A silent one may not.

In the ARIC study, for example, silent heart attacks were linked with a markedly increased risk of death over time. Other research has found that myocardial scars detected by cardiac MRI — even in people who did not know they had a heart attack — predicted worse outcomes.

The key point for patients: **if testing shows you had a prior heart attack, even if you never felt it, doctors generally take it seriously.**

---

## Should everyone be screened for silent heart attacks?

This is where the answer becomes more nuanced.

Doctors do **not** generally recommend that every healthy adult get routine ECGs, stress tests, or heart scans simply to look for a silent heart attack.

Why not?

Because screening can lead to:

- false-positive results  
- unnecessary anxiety  
- additional testing  
- exposure to radiation from some imaging tests  
- procedures that may not improve outcomes in low-risk people  
- incidental findings that are difficult to interpret

The **U.S. Preventive Services Task Force** has recommended against routine ECG screening for coronary heart disease in adults at **low risk** who do not have symptoms. For people at intermediate or high risk, evidence has been less clear, and decisions are usually individualized.

In other words: screening is not one-size-fits-all.

---

## Who should talk to a doctor about evaluation?

People should speak with a clinician if they have symptoms that could suggest heart disease, even if those symptoms are mild or atypical.

That includes:

- chest pressure, tightness, burning, or discomfort  
- unexplained shortness of breath  
- new fatigue with activity  
- unexplained sweating, nausea, or dizziness  
- pain or discomfort in the jaw, neck, back, shoulder, or arm  
- reduced exercise tolerance  
- palpitations or fainting  
- swelling in the legs or symptoms of heart failure

People at higher cardiovascular risk should also discuss prevention and possible testing with their doctor. Risk factors include:

- high blood pressure  
- high LDL cholesterol  
- diabetes  
- smoking  
- obesity  
- chronic kidney disease  
- family history of early heart disease  
- prior stroke or peripheral artery disease  
- sedentary lifestyle  
- sleep apnea

In many cases, the most important “screening” is not an ECG — it’s a comprehensive risk assessment: blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, lifestyle factors, family history, and calculation of 10-year cardiovascular risk.

---

## What should people do to reduce their risk?

Cardiologists emphasize that prevention remains the most powerful strategy.

Steps that lower heart attack risk include:

- not smoking  
- controlling blood pressure  
- treating high cholesterol  
- managing diabetes  
- exercising regularly  
- maintaining a healthy weight  
- eating a heart-healthy diet, such as a Mediterranean-style diet  
- limiting ultra-processed foods and excess sodium  
- getting adequate sleep  
- treating sleep apnea if present  
- taking prescribed medications consistently  
- knowing your family history

For people who have already had a silent heart attack, treatment may be similar to treatment after a recognized heart attack, depending on the patient’s overall condition and test results.

---

## When is it an emergency?

Doctors stress that symptoms should not be ignored just because they are not dramatic.

Call emergency services immediately if you have:

- chest pain or pressure lasting more than a few minutes  
- chest discomfort with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, or faintness  
- pain spreading to the arm, jaw, neck, back, or shoulder  
- sudden severe shortness of breath  
- unexplained collapse or fainting  
- symptoms that feel unusual, intense, or persistent

It is safer to be evaluated and find out it is not a heart attack than to wait and risk permanent heart damage.

---

**ANCHOR:**  
The bottom line: not all heart attacks announce themselves with crushing chest pain. Some are quiet, but the damage can still be real. Researchers say silent heart attacks are linked to a higher risk of death and future heart problems, which is why doctors urge people to know their risk factors, pay attention to unusual symptoms, and talk with a healthcare provider about the right prevention plan.

Routine screening for everyone is not recommended, but targeted evaluation for people with symptoms or elevated risk can be lifesaving.
